Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 44, verse 3–6 (part 1 of 2):

﴿By the Clear Book﴾ [al-Dukhan: 2] ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during a blessed night. Indeed, We were ever warning.﴾ ﴿In it is made distinct every precise matter﴾ ﴿by command from Us. Indeed, We were ever sending [messengers]﴾ ﴿as a mercy from your Lord. Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾

The discussion regarding the like of this oath and its answer has already passed at the beginning of Surah al-Zukhruf.

He highlighted the status of the Qur'an by way of kinaya (allusion) to it, by mentioning the excellence of the time in which its revelation began.

The definiteness of "al-Kitab" is the definiteness of reference (al-'ahd), and what is meant by "al-Kitab" is the Qur'an.

The meaning of the verb in "anzalnahu" is the beginning of its revelation, for every verse or verses that descend from the Qur'an are joined to it in the manner of a part joined to a whole, and the totality that the revelation reaches at every moment is what is named the Qur'an, until the revelation of the last verse of the Qur'an was completed.

The indefiniteness of "laylah" (night) is for glorification, and describing it as "mubarakah" (blessed) is a mark of its esteem and an arousing of desire to know it. This night is the night in which the revelation of the Qur'an to Muhammad (ﷺ) began, in the cave on Mount Hira', in Ramadan. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿The month of Ramadan is that in which the Qur'an was sent down﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185].

The night in which the revelation of the Qur'an began is the Night of Decree (Laylat al-Qadr). God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree﴾ [al-Qadr: 1]. The most correct view is that it is within the last ten nights of Ramadan, and that it is on an odd night. It is established that God made for its counterpart in every year a great excellence, owing to the abundance of the reward of worship in it, every Ramadan, as an honour for the remembrance of the descent of the Qur'an and the beginning of the mission of the best of the messengers (ﷺ) to mankind as a whole. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿The angels and the Spirit descend therein by the permission of their Lord, with every decree. Peace it is until the emergence of dawn﴾ [al-Qadr: 4].
صفحة ٢٧٨
That is among the meanings of its blessing, and how many blessings it has for the Muslims in their religion. Perhaps that blessing extends to their righteous affairs of worldly matters.

The blessing of the night in which the Qur'an was sent down is a blessing that God decreed for it before the descent of the Qur'an, so that by the beginning of the Qur'an's revelation in it, it would be associated with a blessed time, and thus it would increase in excellence and honour. This is one of the subtle divine correspondences of which God has informed us of some.

The apparent meaning is that God renews that blessing in it every year, as indicated by His saying: ﴿The month of Ramadan is that in which the Qur'an was sent down﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185], since He said it after some fifteen years had passed since the beginning of the revelation of the Qur'an. [This is supported also by] His saying: ﴿The Night of Decree is better than a thousand months﴾ [al-Qadr: 3], His saying: ﴿The angels and the Spirit descend therein by the permission of their Lord, with every decree﴾ [al-Qadr: 4], and His saying: ﴿In it is made distinct every precise matter﴾.

It is reported from Ikrimah that the blessed night is the night of the middle of Sha'ban, and this is a weak opinion.

It has been disputed which night of the nights of Ramadan was the one in which the revelation of the Qur'an began upon the Prophet (ﷺ). It was said: it is the seventeenth night of it, as Ibn Ishaq related from al-Baqir, taking it from His saying: ﴿If you have believed in God and in what We sent down upon Our servant on the Day of Criterion, the day the two companies met﴾ [al-Anfal: 41], for the Messenger of God (ﷺ) met the polytheists at Badr on the Friday morning of the seventeenth night of Ramadan. End of quote. That is, he interpreted His saying: ﴿what We sent down upon Our servant﴾ [al-Anfal: 41] as referring to the beginning of the revelation of the Qur'an. Regarding what is meant by "what We sent down" there are possibilities that remove the argument from this interpretation, namely that the beginning of the revelation of the Qur'an was on a night like the night of the Day of Badr.

What must be affirmed with certainty is that the night of the revelation of the Qur'an was in the month of Ramadan, and that it was in the Night of Decree.

Since the reports are numerous that the Prophet (ﷺ) said concerning the Night of Decree: "Seek it in the last ten [nights] of Ramadan: on the third [night remaining], it remains; on the fifth, it remains; on the seventh, it remains; on the ninth, it remains." صفحة ٢٧٩
It has become well known among many Muslims that the Night of Decree is the twenty-seventh night constantly, and this contradicts the hadith "seek it in the last ten" on every interpretation.

The clause "Indeed, We were ever warning" is parenthetical (mu'taridah). The particle "inna" may be for emphasis, in response to their denial that God would send messengers to mankind, since the polytheists denied the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ) on the claim that God does not send a messenger from among humans. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿When they said, "God has not sent down anything upon a human"﴾ [al-An'am: 91]. So the response to their denial of that was a response to their denial of the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ), and thus the clause "Indeed, We were ever warning" is a fresh statement (mustanfa'ah).

It is also possible that "inna" is merely for drawing attention to the report, so that it functions in place of the causal fa' and thus conveys causation. In that case the clause "Indeed, We were ever warning" is a reason for the clause "We sent it down," meaning: We sent it down for warning, because warning is Our concern. The meaning of the clause is a reason for a reason, which is concise expression. He restricted the description to "warners" although the Qur'an warns and gives glad tidings, out of concern for warning, because it is what the condition of most people required at that time, and warning entails glad tidings for whoever heeds it. The object of "warners" is omitted, indicated by His saying "Indeed, We sent it down during a blessed night," meaning: warners to those addressed by the Qur'an.

Its description as "mubarakah," as you have learned just now, indicates the great standing of this night with God, for in it the revelation of the Qur'an appeared, and in it is made distinct, with God, every precise matter.

In these four clauses there is the rhetorical device of laff wa nashr (folding and unfolding). In His saying: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during a blessed night﴾ there is a folding together of two meanings: the first is the specification of the revelation of the Qur'an, and the second is the particularity of its descent in a blessed night. Then he gave a reason for the first meaning with the clause ﴿Indeed, We were ever warning﴾, and gave a reason for the second meaning with the clause ﴿In it is made distinct every precise matter﴾.

Surah al-Ma'idah. That is, God made the night in which the Qur'an was sent down a time for the carrying out and occurrence of important matters, such as the sending of Muhammad (ﷺ), honouring those decreed matters and honouring that night.

God is the One who knows the details of all that.

The repetition of the word "amran" is to magnify its matter; otherwise the primary intended purpose is His saying "from Us," so the apparent arrangement would have been for "min 'indina" to occur as a qualifier of "amrun hakim." This was departed from for this subtle point, namely: a great, majestic matter, when described as "hakim." Then [it is further honoured] by its being from the presence of God, as an honour through this nearness to Him. This honour and magnification primarily and specifically refers to the Qur'an, since its descent in that night is the honouring of that night and making it a time for the decreeing of noble, wise matters.

Know that the opening of the surah may be an address to the polytheists from the outset, to open their insight to the nobility of the Qur'an and the benefit it contains for mankind, so that they may refrain from obstructing others from it. For this reason the disjointed letters occur at its beginning, the purpose of which is the challenge of inimitability, and those three clauses include the particle of emphasis. The informing of the Messenger (ﷺ) of these qualities would be incidental, if his being informed of them had not already preceded through the verses of the Qur'an or through revelation other than the Qur'an.

It is also possible that it is addressed primarily to the Messenger (ﷺ), and the knowledge of the polytheists of what it contains is incidental, by way of allusion (ta'rid), and the emphasis is considered with regard to the allusive purpose.

The object of "mursilin" is omitted, indicated by the root of the active participle, that is: sending the messengers.

And ﴿as a mercy from your Lord﴾ is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu) for ﴿Indeed, We were ever sending [messengers]﴾, meaning: We were sending for the sake of Our mercy, that is, toward the servants to whom the messengers are sent, because sending with warning is a mercy toward people, so that they may avoid the abysses of punishment and acquire the gains of reward. It is also possible that "rahmatan" is a circumstantial state (hal) of the pronoun in "anzalnahu."

The benefit of this explicit mention is to signal that the meaning of lordship calls for mercy upon those who are lordship's charges. Then the attribution of "Rabb" to the pronoun of the Messenger (ﷺ) turns the speech away from addressing the polytheists toward addressing the Prophet (ﷺ) with the discourse, because he is the one through whom their address came, so he is like one present with them at the directing of the address to them. Therefore the direction of the speech is sometimes turned toward him, as in His saying: ﴿Joseph, turn away from this, and you, [O wife], ask forgiveness for your sin﴾ [Yusuf: 29]. This is for the purpose of honouring him after honouring the Book he brought.

And the attribution of "Rabb" to the pronoun of the Messenger (ﷺ) is to achieve a share of honour for him within these legislations, [by indicating] that all of that is from his Lord, that is, through him. For when the sending is a mercy, the Messenger (ﷺ) is a mercy, as God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya': 107]. It is understood from his being the Lord of the Messenger (ﷺ) that He is the Lord of all people, since the Lord cannot be the lord of some people and not others. So it sufficed without saying "a mercy from your Lord and their Lord," because the purpose of attributing "Rabb" to the pronoun of the Messenger (ﷺ) rejects that. Then He will explicitly state that He is their Lord in His saying: ﴿Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers, the first ones﴾ [al-Dukhan: 8], and that is another context whose explanation will come.

The clause ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾ gives the reason for the clause ﴿Indeed, We were sending [messengers] as a mercy from your Lord﴾, meaning: We were sending [messengers] as a mercy to mankind, because He knows the worship of the polytheists of idols, and He knows the misguidance of the leaders of disbelief toward their peoples, and He knows the outcry of people over the oppression of their strong toward their weak, and He knows whatever else is in their statements. So He sent the messengers to set them straight and reform them. He also knows people's intentions, their deeds, and their corruption on earth, so He sent the messengers with the laws (al-shara'i') to restrain people from corruption and to reform their beliefs and their actions. The first kind of knowledge is indicated by the attribute All-Hearing, because the All-Hearing is the one who knows statements, so nothing of them is hidden from Him. The second kind of knowledge is indicated by the attribute All-Knowing, which encompasses all that is known. He placed All-Hearing first because of the concern with what is heard, since the root of disbelief is the supplication of the polytheists to their idols.

Know that All-Hearing and All-Knowing are two reasons for the clause ﴿Indeed, We were sending﴾ by way of symbolic implication (al-kinayah al-ramziyyah), because the real cause of sending is the will for what is good and the mercy toward creation. As for knowledge, it is the attribute by which the will operates in accordance with it. So the reasoning through the attribute of knowledge is based on another premise, namely that God Most High is Wise and does not love corruption. Thus, if He does not love that, and He is All-Knowing of the conduct of creation, His knowledge and His wisdom necessitate that He send messengers to people as a mercy to them.

The pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl) conveys restriction (al-hasr), meaning: He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing, not your idols that you invoke.

In this there is an indication of the need for sending a messenger to them, to nullify the worship of idols.

In the description All-Hearing, All-Knowing there is an allusive threat (ta'rid bi'l-tahdid).

It is also possible that it is addressed primarily to the Messenger (ﷺ), and the knowledge of the polytheists of what it contains is incidental, by way of allusion (ta'rid), and the emphasis is considered with regard to the allusive purpose.

The object of "mursilin" is omitted, indicated by the root of the active participle, that is: sending the messengers.

And ﴿as a mercy from your Lord﴾ is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu) for ﴿Indeed, We were ever sending [messengers]﴾, meaning: We were sending for the sake of Our mercy, that is, toward the servants to whom the messengers are sent, because sending with warning is a mercy toward people, so that they may avoid the abysses of punishment and acquire the gains of reward. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya': 107]. It is also possible that "rahmatan" is a circumstantial state (hal) of the pronoun in "anzalnahu."

The mention of the word "Rabb" (Lord) in His saying "from your Lord" is an explicit noun in place of the pronoun, since the apparent arrangement would have been to say: "a mercy from Us." The benefit of this explicit mention is to signal that the meaning of lordship calls for mercy upon those who are lordship's charges. Then the attribution of "Rabb" to the pronoun of the Messenger (ﷺ) turns the speech away from addressing the polytheists toward addressing the Prophet (ﷺ) with the discourse, because he is the one through whom their address came, so he is like one present with them at the directing of the address to them. Therefore the direction of the speech is sometimes turned toward him, as in His saying: ﴿Joseph, turn away from this, and you, [O wife], ask forgiveness for your sin﴾ [Yusuf: 29]. This is for the purpose of honouring him after honouring the Book he brought.

And the attribution of "Rabb" to the pronoun of the Messenger (ﷺ) is to achieve a share of honour for him within these legislations, [by indicating] that all of that is from his Lord, that is, through him. For when the sending is a mercy, the Messenger (ﷺ) is a mercy, as God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya': 107]. It is understood from his being the Lord of the Messenger (ﷺ) that He is the Lord of all people, since the Lord cannot be the lord of some people and not others. So it sufficed without saying "a mercy from your Lord and their Lord," because the purpose of attributing "Rabb" to the pronoun of the Messenger (ﷺ) rejects that. Then He will explicitly state that He is their Lord in His saying: ﴿Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers, the first ones﴾ [al-Dukhan: 8], and that is another context whose explanation will come.

The clause ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾ gives the reason for the clause ﴿Indeed, We were sending [messengers] as a mercy from your Lord﴾, meaning: We were sending [messengers] as a mercy to mankind, because He knows the worship of the polytheists of idols, and He knows the misguidance of the leaders of disbelief toward their peoples, and He knows the outcry of people over the oppression of their strong toward their weak, and He knows whatever else is in their statements. So He sent the messengers to set them straight and reform them. He also knows people's intentions, their deeds, and their corruption on earth, so He sent the messengers with the laws (al-shara'i') to restrain people from corruption and to reform their beliefs and their actions. The first kind of knowledge is indicated by the attribute All-Hearing, because the All-Hearing is the one who knows statements, so nothing of them is hidden from Him. The second kind of knowledge is indicated by the attribute All-Knowing, which encompasses all that is known. He placed All-Hearing first because of the concern with what is heard, since the root of disbelief is the supplication of the polytheists to their idols.

Know that All-Hearing and All-Knowing are two reasons for the clause ﴿Indeed, We were sending﴾ by way of symbolic implication (al-kinayah al-ramziyyah), because the real cause of sending is the will for what is good and the mercy toward creation. As for knowledge, it is the attribute by which the will operates in accordance with it. So the reasoning through the attribute of knowledge is based on another premise, namely that God Most High is Wise and does not love corruption. Thus, if He does not love that, and He is All-Knowing of the conduct of creation, His knowledge and His wisdom necessitate that He send messengers to people as a mercy to them.

The pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl) conveys restriction (al-hasr), meaning: He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing, not your idols that you invoke.

In this there is an indication of the need for sending a messenger to them, to nullify the worship of idols.

In the description All-Hearing, All-Knowing there is an allusive threat (ta'rid bi'l-tahdid).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 44, verse 7:

Page 283
﴿The Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, if you are certain.﴾

This is a return to confronting the polytheists with admonition, in the same manner with which the surah began.

It is a transition (takhallus) to the argument for God's sole divinity (tafarrud Allah bil-ilahiyyah), as a reproach to them with what they acknowledge: that He is the Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, and they acknowledge that the idols do not create anything. Yet they turn away from the conclusion of the proof, which is the invalidity of the divinity of the idols. Do you not see that the Qur'an repeats its admonition to them with the like of this, such as His saying, ﴿Is He who creates like He who does not create? Will you not remember?﴾ [al-Nahl: 17], and His saying, ﴿And those whom you invoke besides God create nothing, and they are created. They are dead, not alive﴾ [al-Nahl: 20]. For this reason He mentioned lordship in summary in His saying, ﴿a mercy from your Lord﴾, then in detail by mentioning the attribute of all-encompassing knowledge, which is the attribute of the one truly worshipped, in the form of qasr al-qalb (restriction by reversal), indicating that the idols neither hear nor know. And by mentioning the attribute of creation, which is exclusive to Him, the Exalted, with their admission, as an ascent in the argument. So when there was no room for doubt that He, the Exalted, is the true God, He followed this argument with the clause ﴿if you are certain﴾, in a manner that stirs their minds to awareness, since He treated them as those whose certainty is doubtful, because they do not act according to the requirement of certainty that God is the Creator, when they worship other than Him. It was expressed in the form of a condition, on the assumption of their certainty, and the particle of condition was used, whose original meaning is the absence of certainty that the condition will occur, as in His saying, ﴿Shall We then turn away the reminder from you altogether because you are a people who exceed the limits?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 5].

The majority (al-Jumhur) read (Rabbu al-samawati) with the nominative ending on Rabb, as the predicate of an omitted subject (mubtada' mahdhuf), and this is from the omission of the subject (hadhf al-musnad ilayhi) to follow the usage in such cases, after stating predicates or attributes of a thing and then adding another predicate. From this is the saying, after mentioning a person: "A youth who does and does" (fata yaf'alu wa yaf'alu). It is also an explanatory resumption (al-isti'naf al-bayani), as the implied meaning is: if you wish to know Him, then He is such-and-such. ʿĀṣim, Ḥamzah, al-Kisā'ī and Khalaf read (Rabbi) with the genitive ending, as a substitute (badal) for His saying ﴿your Lord﴾.

The complement of (muqinin) is omitted because it is known from His saying ﴿the Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them﴾. The answer of the condition is omitted, indicated by the context. The implied meaning is: if you are certain, then do not worship other than Him, and for this reason He followed it with the clause ﴿there is no god but He﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 44, verse 8:

﴿There is no deity except Him; He gives life and causes death. Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers, the first ones.﴾ The clause "There is no deity except Him" is a conclusion (natijah) drawn from the preceding proof, because His sole lordship (rububiyyah) over the heavens and the earth and what is between them is a proof of His sole deity (ilahiyyah), meaning that the deity of their idols is void. Therefore this clause is a conclusion from that, and for this reason it is separated (from what precedes), owing to the strong implication of the preceding clause for it.

The clause "He gives life and causes death" is a resumptive clause (musta'nafah) serving as evidence that there is no deity except Him, by His sole power over giving life and causing death. The polytheists do not dispute that God is the One who gives life and causes death. Just as He was argued against them by His sole bringing into existence of the worlds and what is in them, so He is argued against them by the creation of the greatest state of existing things, which is the state of life, with which man was honoured above the beings of the terrestrial world, and which was also bestowed upon animals, honoured by being subjected for man's benefit through them; and by His sole power over causing death, which is the removal of life from the living, to indicate that life is not inherent in the living.

Since His sole power over giving life and causing death is a clear proof in the circumstances of the addressees and in what surrounds them, namely the appearance of the living through birth and the dead through decease, day after day, it is fitting that they should not be ignorant of its indication, let alone deny it. Yet despite this they worshipped idols that neither give life nor cause death. He therefore followed up with the affirmation of His lordship over the addressees, as a record against them for denying the proofs and for ingratitude for the blessing.

He conjoined "and the Lord of your forefathers, the first ones" in order to record against them the obligation implied by their saying, ﴿Indeed we found our fathers upon a religion, and indeed we are following in their footsteps, guided﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 22]. He described them as "the first ones" because they made the most ancient of the forefathers a greater proof than the nearer forefathers, as God, exalted is He, said quoting them: ﴿We have not heard of this among our first forefathers﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 24].

(بَلْ) is for *al-idrab al-ibtali* (a turn of speech that cancels what came before), by which it is refuted that they would be certain and affirming that He is the Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them. Their affirmation does not proceed from knowledge and firm certainty; rather it is as nothing, because they mixed it with doubt and play. So the property of certainty and affirmation, which is acting upon the requirement of knowledge, was lifted from it, for knowledge that does not draw its possessor to act upon it and to renew attention to it

[p. 285]

is overtaken first by heedlessness and then by forgetfulness, so it weakens until it becomes doubt, because the proofs by which it would settle in the soul have been veiled. That is, they are doubters concerning the oneness of God, exalted is He.

The use of the particle of place (*harf al-zarfiyyah*, the preposition fi) indicates the intensity with which doubt has taken hold of their souls, to the point that it is as if it were an encompassing vessel around them from which they find no way out. That is, doubt does not leave them. The sense of place here is a *isti'arah tab'iyyah* (a dependent metaphor), like the sense of elevation in His saying ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5].

The clause (يَلْعَبُونَ, *yal'abun*, "they play") is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring to the pronoun in (هم, *hum*, "they"). That is, they have busied themselves, with mockery and play in receiving the call of the Messenger (ﷺ), away from considering the proofs that would remove doubt from them and make them guided. So their immersion in doubt is accompanied by their state of play. This circumstantial clause has a great effect, for it conveys that doubt drives them to mockery and play, and that occupation with play increases doubt in them and makes it more firmly rooted. This is unlike if it had been said: (بَلْ هم في شَكٍّ ولَعِبٍ, *bal hum fi shakkin wa la'ibin*), so reflect on this.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 44, verses 10–11:

﴿So watch for the day when the sky brings a manifest smoke,﴾ ﴿enveloping the people. This is a painful torment.﴾

This is a consequence (tafri') of the statement ﴿Nay, they are in doubt, playing,﴾ [al-Dukhan: 9]. Its purpose is to promise the Messenger ﷺ that God will avenge him against those who deny him, and to warn the polytheists for their denial of the proofs of God's oneness and of the truthfulness of the Messenger, and for their absorption in play, i.e., mockery of the Qur'an and the Messenger. It mentions for them things that frighten the polytheists, to prepare them for faith, and a striking act of vengeance against their leaders that will uproot them.

The address in "watch" (irtaqib) is to the Prophet ﷺ, and the imperative is used to strengthen (tathbit) him. Al-irtiqab (a reflexive form, ifti'al) comes from raqaba, meaning to wait for him; waiting occurs only when the awaited thing is near. The verb "watch" (irtaqib), by its explicit meaning, implies that the coming of the sky with smoke had not yet taken place at the time this verse was revealed, and by implication it indicates that its occurrence is imminent, as one who approaches from a nearby place is awaited.

"Yawm" (day) is a noun of time in the accusative, functioning as the direct object of "watch," not as an adverb of time. This is like His saying, ﴿They fear a day﴾ [al-Nur: 37]. It is annexed (mudaf) to the clause after it, to distinguish the intended day from the rest of the days, namely that it is the one on which the sky brings a manifest smoke. Thus "yawm" is in the accusative in its grammatical case (nasb i'rab) and is not nunated because of the annexation.

A clause to which a noun of time is annexed does not require a connecting pronoun (rabit), because the annexation suffices in place of it, and because the clause has the force of a verbal noun (masdar). The estimated meaning is: "So watch for the day of the sky's coming with smoke."

The word "day" is used for time in general, since the appearance of the smoke occurred over many days and months.

"Al-dukhan" (smoke) is what rises when firewood is kindled, and this is an eloquent metaphor, i.e., like smoke.

"Mubin" means clear and evident; it is an active participle from abana, which has the meaning of bana. The meaning is that it is apparent to everyone, such that no one doubts seeing it.

Abu 'Ubayda and Ibn Qutayba said: the smoke in the verse is the dust that rises from the earth because of drought, and that the Arabs call dust "smoke," namely the dust stirred up by winds from very dry ground.

From al-A'raj: it is the dust raised by the hooves of horses on the day of the Conquest of Mecca, when the dust veiled the sky. Attributing the coming to the sky is an intellectual metaphor (majaz 'aqli), because the sky is its place when it rises into the atmosphere of the sky, or when it appears to the eyes from it.

The discourse indicates that this awaited smoke is an event near at hand, so the apparent meaning is that it is an occurrence in this worldly life, and that it is a punishment for the polytheists.

By "the people" in His saying ﴿enveloping the people﴾ is meant the polytheists, as is the usual use of the word "people" in the Qur'an. It also indicates that it lifts from them for a short time as an excuse for them, perhaps they will believe, and that they return after its lifting to what they were upon, and that God sends it back upon them, as His saying indicates: ﴿Indeed, We will remove the punishment a little, but you will return﴾ [al-Dukhan: 15]. As for His saying ﴿the day We seize with the greatest seizing﴾ [al-Dukhan: 16], it is another punishment. All of this indicates that the punishment by smoke occurs in this world and is a near future. Since the verse is Meccan, it is established that this smoke, which is a punishment for the polytheists, does not strike the believers, by His saying ﴿God would not punish them while you are among them, nor is God going to punish them while they seek forgiveness﴾ [al-Anfal: 33]. Thus it is established that the believers on the day of this smoke were not residing in the land of polytheism. So this smoke necessarily occurred after the Hijra, and it is established that it occurred before the polytheists of Mecca and its surroundings embraced Islam, so it is established that it occurred before the Conquest of Mecca or on the day of the Conquest, according to differing opinions.

The most correct view is that by this smoke is meant what befell the polytheists of the years of famine in Mecca after the Prophet's ﷺ Hijra to Medina. The most sound report on this is the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud in Sahih al-Bukhari, from Muslim and Abu al-Duha, from Masruq, who said: "I entered upon 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud and he said: 'When the Quraysh overcame the Prophet ﷺ and disobeyed him, he said: O God, help me against them with seven years like the seven of Joseph. So a year of famine seized them, in which they ate bones and carrion from hardship, until one of them would see between himself and the sky something like smoke from hunger. The Messenger of God ﷺ was approached and it was said to him: Ask rain for Mudar, that the punishment be lifted from them. So he prayed, and it was lifted from them, and God said to him: If We lift the punishment from them they will return. So they returned, and God took vengeance upon them on the day of Badr. That is His saying: ﴿So watch for the day when the sky brings a manifest smoke﴾ up to His saying ﴿the day We seize with the greatest seizing, indeed We will take vengeance﴾ [al-Dukhan: 16]. And the greatest seizing is the day of Badr.'" And 'Abd Allah said: Five have passed: the smoke, the Romans, the moon, the seizing, and the lazam (inevitable punishment).

In the hadith of Abu Hurayra in Sahih al-Bukhari, in the chapters on seeking rain: "The Prophet ﷺ, when he raised his head from the last rak'a of the dawn prayer, would say: O God, deliver 'Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'a. O God, deliver Salama ibn Hisham. O God, deliver al-Walid ibn al-Walid. O God, deliver the weak among the believers. O God, tighten Your grip upon Mudar. O God, make it upon them years like the years of Joseph." Those for whom he prayed for deliverance were among those whom the polytheists had imprisoned after the Hijra. All these reports indicate that the Prophet's ﷺ supplication against the polytheists with years of famine was after the Hijra, so that the Muslims would not be punished with hunger, and that it was before the Battle of Badr. In some reports of the qunut, he prayed in the qunut against Banu Lihyan and 'Usayya.

What is derived from the reports is that this hunger befell the Quraysh shortly after the Hijra, and that is the hunger for which the Prophet ﷺ prayed when he said: "O God, help me against them with seven years like the seven of Joseph." In another report: "O God, tighten Your grip upon Mudar, O God, make it upon them years like the years of Joseph. Then the Prophet ﷺ was approached and it was said to him: Ask rain for Mudar." In a report from Masruq from Ibn Mas'ud in Sahih al-Bukhari, the one who came to the Prophet was Abu Sufyan. The exegetes said: Abu Sufyan came to him with some people from Mecca, meaning they came to Medina when they learned that the Prophet had prayed against them for drought, and they said: "Your people have perished, so pray to God that He give them rain," and he prayed.

According to this report, His saying ﴿the day the sky brings a manifest smoke﴾ is an image of the state of what the hungry see, like a veil over their eyes when they look at the air, in the form of smoke descending from the horizon. So the metaphor lies in the composition (al-majaz fi al-tarkib). As for the individual words of the composition, they are used in their literal meanings, because among the meanings of "sky" in the speech of the Arabs is the dome of the air. The clause ﴿enveloping the people﴾ serves as a continuation (tarshih) of the imagery, because what envelops them is the darkness in their eyes from hunger, not the smoke that envelops them.

Some reports attached to this verse the hadith of rain-seeking found in the Sahih: "A man came on Friday while the Prophet ﷺ was giving the sermon and said: O Messenger of God, the crops and the livestock have perished, so pray to God that He give us rain. He raised his hands and said: O God, give us rain, three times. There was not seen in the sky a wisp of cloud, but the sky became thick with clouds, and they were given rain from Friday to Friday, until the valleys flowed and the valley of Qanat flowed for a month. Then a messenger came the next Friday, he was the first or another, and said: O Messenger of God, the roads have been cut off, so pray to God that He hold back the rain from us. He said: O God, around us and not upon us. So the clouds dispersed until Medina was like a crown of cloud."

The combination of the two reports is evident. It appears that this famine occurred after the Battle of Badr, so it is another famine, different from the famine of the Quraysh mentioned in this verse.

The meaning of ﴿enveloping the people﴾ is that it surrounds them and covers them as a covering envelops the body, i.e., none of those people, namely the polytheists, escapes from it. If what is meant by the smoke is what befell their sight, a sight like a dust-cloud from hunger, then "enveloping" is a metaphor. If what is meant by it is the dust of war on the day of the Conquest, then "enveloping" is literal or a well-known metaphor. It is also possible that it is dust rising into the air from the severe dryness.

As for His saying ﴿This is a painful torment﴾, Ibn 'Atiyya said: it may be a statement from God, the Exalted, expressing wonder at it, as in His saying in the story of the sacrifice: ﴿Indeed, this is the manifest trial﴾ [al-Saffat: 106]. It is also possible that this is the saying of the people whom the torment envelops, with the estimate: they say, "This is a painful torment."

The demonstrative in ﴿This is a painful torment﴾ refers to the smoke mentioned just before. He turned away from bringing it to mind by the pronoun, and from saying "it is a painful torment," to bringing it to mind by the demonstrative, placing it in the position of something present and witnessed, to magnify its matter, as you say: "This winter is coming, so prepare for it."

Close to this is the command to look in His saying ﴿See how they lied against themselves﴾ [al-An'am: 24], for what is related there is what occurs in the Hereafter.

In another report: "O God, tighten Your grip upon Mudar, O God, make it upon them years like the years of Joseph. Then the Prophet ﷺ was approached and it was said to him: Ask rain for Mudar." In a report from Masruq from Ibn Mas'ud in Sahih al-Bukhari, the one who came to the Prophet was Abu Sufyan. The exegetes said: Abu Sufyan came to him with some people from Mecca, meaning they came to Medina when they learned that the Prophet had prayed against them for drought, and they said: "Your people have perished, so pray to God that He give them rain," and he prayed.

According to this report, His saying ﴿the day the sky brings a manifest smoke﴾ is an image of the state of what the hungry see, like a veil over their eyes when they look at the air, in the form of smoke descending from the horizon. So the metaphor lies in the composition (al-majaz fi al-tarkib). As for the individual words of the composition, they are used in their literal meanings, because among the meanings of "sky" in the speech of the Arabs is the dome of the air. The clause ﴿enveloping the people﴾ serves as a continuation (tarshih) of the imagery, because what envelops them is the darkness in their eyes from hunger, not the smoke that envelops them.

Some reports attached to this verse the hadith of rain-seeking found in the Sahih: "A man came on Friday while the Prophet ﷺ was giving the sermon and said: O Messenger of God, the crops and the livestock have perished, so pray to God that He give us rain. He raised his hands and said: O God, give us rain, three times. There was not seen in the sky a wisp of cloud, but the sky became thick with clouds, and they were given rain from Friday to Friday, until the valleys flowed and the valley of Qanat flowed for a month. Then a messenger came the next Friday, he was the first or another, and said: O Messenger of God, the roads have been cut off, so pray to God that He hold back the rain from us. He said: O God, around us and not upon us. So the clouds dispersed until Medina was like a crown of cloud."

The combination of the two reports is evident. It appears that this famine occurred after the Battle of Badr, so it is another famine, different from the famine of the Quraysh mentioned in this verse.

The meaning of ﴿enveloping the people﴾ is that it surrounds them and covers them as a covering envelops the body, i.e., none of those people, namely the polytheists, escapes from it. If what is meant by the smoke is what befell their sight, a sight like a dust-cloud from hunger, then "enveloping" is a metaphor. If what is meant by it is the dust of war on the day of the Conquest, then "enveloping" is literal or a well-known metaphor. It is also possible that it is dust rising into the air from the severe dryness.

As for His saying ﴿This is a painful torment﴾, Ibn 'Atiyya said: it may be a statement from God, the Exalted, expressing wonder at it, as in His saying in the story of the sacrifice: ﴿Indeed, this is the manifest trial﴾ [al-Saffat: 106]. It is also possible that this is the saying of the people whom the torment envelops, with the estimate: they say, "This is a painful torment."

The demonstrative in ﴿This is a painful torment﴾ refers to the smoke mentioned just before. He turned away from bringing it to mind by the pronoun, and from saying "it is a painful torment," to bringing it to mind by the demonstrative, placing it in the position of something present and witnessed, to magnify its matter, as you say: "This winter is coming, so prepare for it."

Close to this is the command to look in His saying ﴿See how they lied against themselves﴾ [al-An'am: 24], for what is related there is what occurs in the Hereafter.

**[Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur, *al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir*, on Surah al-Dukhan (chapter 44), verse 12]**

﴿Our Lord, remove the punishment from us; indeed we are believers.﴾

This is a parenthetical clause (*mu'tarida*) placed between the clause ﴿This is a painful punishment﴾ [al-Dukhan: 11] and the clause ﴿How will they have the reminder?﴾ [al-Dukhan: 13]. It is therefore the content of an implied saying (*maqul qawl mahdhuf*).

All the exegetes took it to be a report of the words of those who are overcome by the punishment, with the implied verb "they say": ﴿Our Lord, remove the punishment from us﴾. That is, it is a promise made by the people overtaken by the punishment that they will believe if the punishment is lifted from them. (This is like His saying in Surah al-Zukhruf: ﴿They said, "O sorcerer, call upon your Lord for us by what He has covenanted with you; indeed we will be guided."﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 49], meaning: if you call upon your Lord, we will follow you.) It may also correspond to His saying in Surah al-A'raf: ﴿And when the punishment fell upon them, they said, "O Moses, call upon your Lord for us"﴾ [al-A'raf: 134], up to His saying ﴿"If you remove the punishment from us, we will surely believe in you"﴾ [al-A'raf: 134].

Among the things that the structure of the verse and its context allow is that the implied saying is in the form of an imperative, meaning: "Say," as a means of instructing the Muslims to seek refuge in God from the punishment befalling them while they were in the same land as the polytheists. This is like Musa (peace be upon him) seeking refuge with his words: ﴿Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us did?﴾ [al-A'raf: 155]. There is in this an allusion (*ima'*) that God will bring the believers out of Mecca before this punishment descends upon its people. This instruction is like His saying: ﴿Our Lord, do not hold us accountable if we forget or err﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286], and the verses that follow.

Accordingly, the clause ﴿indeed we are believers﴾ is a reason (*ta'lil*) for the request to avert the punishment from them, meaning: indeed we are characterised by that which averts from us the punishment of the disbelievers. Teaching them to say this is an honouring of the excellence of faith.

The construction of the speech is also consistent with the view that the clause ﴿indeed we are believers﴾ gives the reason for the request to lift the punishment from them, as indicated by the apparent meaning of the use of the particle *inna* (indeed) in conveying information rather than a promise, and in giving a reason rather than emphasis; and as indicated by the active participle (*ism al-fa'il*), which denotes the present tense rather than the future; and because its context is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ) while he awaits God's help against the polytheists, as he used to pray against them, saying: "O Allah, make them (years) like the years of Yusuf." The requirement of the situation is therefore to assure him that the punishment will not befall the Muslims while the Prophet (ﷺ) is among them.

The apparent sense of the root *k-sh-f* (to uncover, to remove) is the removal of something that was present upon something. However, since *al-kashf* is not used here in its literal meaning, its figurative usage (*majaz*) may be understood as preventing something from occurring that is feared to occur, as in His saying: ﴿Except the people of Yunus: when they believed, We removed from them the punishment of disgrace in the worldly life﴾ [Yunus: 98]. The people of Yunus had not been struck by the punishment, so it did not "leave" them; rather, they were threatened with it, so they hastened to faith, and God saved them from it. It is also possible that the usage means the removal of something that had already occurred.

Consider the verse of Ja'far ibn 'Ulba al-Harithi:

*None removes the distress except the son of a free woman,*
*who sees the throes of death and then visits them.*

He meant that he prevents the enemy from reaching them with harm, and this is also possible in the sense of removing something that had already occurred.

None of the transmitters of the biographical reports (*siyar*) and narrations (*athar*) has mentioned that the polytheists promised the Prophet (ﷺ) that they would embrace Islam if God removed the famine from them.

Verse 13–14:

﴿How can they [benefit from] the reminder, when there has come to them a clear Messenger?﴾ ﴿Then they turned away from him and said, "[He is] one taught [by others], a madman."﴾

All the exegetes took this sentence as a reply to the words of those who say, "Our Lord, remove the punishment from us; indeed we are believers," as a denial of their promise. That is, they will not take heed. And how would they take heed, when there has come to them something more evident as proof than the punishment, namely the evidences of the truthfulness of the Messenger ﷺ? As for the interpretation that we have derived from the composition of the verse, it is a resumptive sentence (jumlah mustanfa'ah) arising from His words, "Rather, they are in doubt, playing," and it is like a conclusion (natījah) to it, because when they are in doubt and playing, they have become remote from the reminder.

"Anna" (أنّى) is an interrogative noun whose original sense is asking about the places where a thing occurs. They extend its use, making it an interrogative about states, in the sense of "how" (kayfa), by treating states as if they were places, as here, as indicated by His words, "and there has come to them a clear Messenger." The meaning: from where would the reminder and the fear be attained for them at the appearance of the manifest smoke, when the paths to it have been blocked by their slandering of the Messenger ﷺ who came to them with the reminder?

The interrogation is used in the sense of denial and improbability, that is, how could they take heed when they are in doubt, playing, and there has come to them a clear Messenger, so they turned away from him and slandered him. Thus the clause "and there has come to them" is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

"Mubīn" is an active participle, either from abāna (transitive), whose object is omitted because the reminder indicates it, meaning "making clear to them what they would take heed by"; or it may be from abāna (intransitive), which has the sense of bāna, meaning "a manifest Messenger," that is, his message is manifest as from God, with the evidences of his truthfulness abundantly accompanying it.

The preference for "mubīn" with a light yā' over "mubayyin" with a doubled yā' is among the subtleties of inimitability, so that it conveys both meanings.

"Thumma" (ثُمَّ) here indicates rank-based sequence (al-tarākhī al-rutbī), an ascent from the implication of His words, "Rather, they are in doubt, playing," to which the clause is connected; the clause "and there has come to them a clear Messenger" was among its related elements. The meaning: a Messenger has come to them, so they doubted his mission, then they turned away from him and slandered him. The turning away and the slander occurred upon the occurrence of doubt and play, and for this reason "thumma" is for rank-based sequence, not for temporal sequence. The sense of rank-based sequence here is that turning away and calumny are more heinous than doubt and play.

"Mu'allim" is one who is taught by another; it was mentioned earlier at His words, "We know that they say, 'Only a human teaches him'" [al-Naḥl: 103], in Surat al-Naḥl.

The meaning: they described him once as being taught by another, and described him once as a madman, shifting about in their calumny; or one group described him with this and another group with that. Thus the statement is distributed between the speakers of the pronoun in "qālū," or between the times of the speakers. It is not valid that it be one statement at one time, because a madman cannot be one who is taught, nor is he affected by instruction.

Ibn 'Ashur, *al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir*, commentary on Surah 44, verse 15:

﴿Indeed, We will remove the punishment a little, but you will surely revert.﴾ This follows what all the exegetes (*mufassirun*) have explained, that His words ﴿Our Lord, remove from us the punishment﴾ are the subject of their request, and that this sentence is an answer to their request. It also follows what we have adopted: that this sentence is an announcement to the Prophet ﷺ that He will remove the punishment with which the polytheists were threatened for a period, after which they will return to what they were doing. On this view, the pronoun in ﴿you will surely revert﴾ is a shift (*iltifat*, a change of grammatical address) to addressing the polytheists. That is, they will refrain from that for a period, namely the period in which they sent their delegation to Medina so that the Messenger ﷺ would ask God to remove the drought from them. During those days they refrained from reproach and abuse, hoping that he would pray for them, and then they returned to what they had been doing. This is like the saying of the Exalted: ﴿When harm touches a man, he calls upon his Lord, turning to Him in repentance; then when He bestows on him a favor from Him, he forgets what he was calling upon Him for before, and sets up rivals to God to lead others astray from His way﴾ [al-Zumar: 8]. Likewise, it implies that the punishment will return upon them after they return to what they were doing of the causes of their being struck by the punishment.

So the meaning of ﴿Indeed, We are removers of the punishment﴾ is: We will remove it in the future, by the indication of His words before it, ﴿So watch for the day when the sky brings forth a manifest smoke﴾, which requires that it occurs in the future. The verses are connected to one another, and likewise the meaning of ﴿you will surely revert﴾ is that it occurs in the future. The active participle (*ism al-fa'il*) may be intended to denote occurrence in the future, by the indication of context.

It is related that the drought was removed from them after the Prophet ﷺ prayed for rain, so they lived and their livestock lived, but then they returned, and the drought afflicted them again for seven years. Perhaps the conquest of Mecca followed it.

The sentence ﴿you will surely revert﴾ is a resumptive sentence of explanation (*istinaf bayani*), because when they heard ﴿Indeed, We are removers of the punishment a little﴾, they would look forward to what would happen after its removal, and the believers would look forward to what the state of the polytheists would become after the removal of the punishment, whether they would desist from reproach. So His words ﴿you will surely revert﴾ explain what they were asking about.

﴿On the Day We will seize with the great seizing; indeed, We will take retribution.﴾

This is the retribution that the Messenger (ﷺ) was promised, and with which the leaders of disbelief were threatened.

The sentence is a resumptive sentence (*istīʾnāf*, a sentence begun afresh) of the explanatory kind (*bayānī*, one that clarifies), arising from His saying: ﴿Indeed, We will remove the punishment a little; indeed, you will return [to disbelief].﴾ [Al-Dukhan: 15]. The listener is moved to ask in his soul about their recompense when they return to turning away and to slandering. So he is answered that the retribution against them is the great seizing, which is complete retribution. Because of this longing and questioning, the sentence is emphasised with a predicate and the particle of emphasis (*inna*), to dispel hesitation.

The underlying structure of the sentence is: إنّا مُنْتَقِمُونَ يَوْمَ نَبْطِشُ البَطْشَةَ الكُبْرى. So يَوْمَ is in the accusative as an adverb of time (*maf'ūl fīhi*) governed by the active participle (*ism al-fāʿil*) مُنْتَقِمُونَ.

It has been placed before its governing word for the sake of giving it importance, and to magnify its terror. What prevents this from being an obstacle is that the governing element in the adverb is the predicate of إنَّ, on the basis of the common opinion of the grammarians that what follows إنَّ does not govern what precedes it; adverbs and the like are treated with latitude.

The great seizing (البَطْشَةُ الكُبْرى) is the seizing of the Day of Badr, for what befell the chieftains of the polytheists on that day was a seizing against polytheism and its people, because they lost their masters and the people of judgement among them, who used to direct the people of Makkah as they wished.

The word البَطْشَةُ is the singular of البَطْشِ, which is: a strong seizing with violence. It has been discussed previously in His saying: ﴿Or do they have hands with which they strike?﴾ [Al-A'raf: 195], in Surat al-A'raf.

[p. 295]

God made the story of Pharaoh's people with Moses, peace be upon him, and the Children of Israel a parable for the state of the polytheists (al-mushrikūn) toward the Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers in him. He made what befell them a warning of what would befall the polytheists of famine and severe seizure, with the nearness of that event, its possibility, and its ease, even though they were in a state of strength, for God is capable of overpowering them. As He said, ﴿So We destroyed those who were mightier than them in strength﴾ [Q. 40:21]. Mentioning it here is therefore a confirmation for the Prophet, a promise to him of victory and a good outcome, and a threat to the polytheists.

Although this parable is a comparison of the whole situation with the whole situation, it admits of distribution (tawzī'), so that Abū Jahl may be compared with Pharaoh, his followers with Pharaoh's chiefs and people, or Muḥammad (ﷺ) with Moses, peace be upon him, and the Muslims with the Children of Israel. Admitting the parable to distribution of the comparison is one of its excellences.

The clause ﴿And We had already tested﴾ may be in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), so that the waw is for the circumstance, and it is a circumstance of the pronoun in ﴿We are avengers﴾ [Q. 44:16].

It may also be conjoined to the clause ﴿We are avengers﴾, meaning: We shall avenge Ourselves on them in the future, and We avenged Ourselves on the people of Pharaoh in the past.

His saying ﴿before them﴾ indicates that the people of Makkah would be tested as the people of Pharaoh were tested. This adverbial phrase therefore signals an elided clause by way of concision (ījāz), the implied sense being: ﴿We are avengers, so tempt them, for We had already tested before them the people of Pharaoh.﴾ It also signals that what is mentioned serves as evidence for the expectation of that event and its possibility, which is another instance of concision.

The intended meaning is to compare the situation with the situation, but the discourse was turned away from the form of comparison and parable to the form of narration, out of concern for the story and to show that in itself it is something worth knowing, that it is an independent reminder, and that it does not depend on anything else.

Also, the clause ﴿and there had come to them a noble messenger﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿We tested﴾, that is: ﴿and there had indeed come to them a noble messenger.﴾ This is the conjunction of the detailed to the summarised. It is conjoined because what is mentioned in it contains more than the meaning of the trial. The clause ﴿and there came to them a noble messenger﴾ is therefore not an explanation of ﴿We tested﴾; rather it is a detailed account of the sending of Moses, peace be upon him.

Al-fatn (trial) means bringing about disorder in conditions. It was discussed earlier in His saying, ﴿and trial is worse than killing﴾, in Surat al-Baqarah.

The noble messenger is Moses. Al-karīm means the precious, the excellent in its kind. It was discussed earlier at His saying, ﴿Indeed, there has been delivered to me a noble letter﴾ [Q. 27:29], in Surat al-Naml, that is: a messenger from the best of the messengers or from the best of people.

His saying ﴿that deliver to me the servants of God﴾ is an explanation of what is contained in the description "messenger" and the verb "came to them" in terms of the meaning of conveying the message and communicating it, so both contain the sense of speech.

The meaning of "deliver to me" (addū ilayya) is: return to me and hand over. He said, ﴿And among them is he who, if you entrust him with a dinar, will not return it to you﴾ [Q. 3:75]. It is said: adda al-shay' (he delivered the thing), meaning he conveyed it and brought it to its destination. The hamza of the verb is original, and it is a verb with a doubled middle radical, and no unduplicated form of it has been heard. He made the Children of Israel like a trust with Pharaoh, in the manner of an implicit metaphor (istiʿāra makniyya).

The address in the plural is to the people of Pharaoh. What is meant is Pharaoh and those of his chiefs who were present, perhaps they would advise Pharaoh toward the truth. Perhaps he addressed the whole body of chiefs because he saw in Pharaoh arrogance and pride that refused compliance, so he addressed his council, perhaps among them there would be one who perceives the truth.

"The servants of God" may be the object of "deliver", with the Children of Israel intended by it. Their description as "servants of God" was given as a reminder to Pharaoh, in accordance with the lifting of enslavement from them. In Surat al-Shu'arā' it came: ﴿Send with us the Children of Israel﴾ [Q. 26:17]. It follows that he described them with both descriptions. The description "servants of God" nullifies the Copts' reckoning of them as slaves, as He said, ﴿and their people are servants to us﴾ [Q. 23:47]. They are in truth servants of God, that is, free people. "Servants of God" is thus a kināya (allusion, metonymy) for freedom, like the saying of Bashshār addressing himself:

"You have become the client of the Lord of Majesty, while some people are the clients of slaves; so seek refuge in His favour and take pride."

It is also possible that the object of the verb "deliver" is elided, indicated by the context, the sense being: ﴿deliver to me obedience﴾, and "servants of God" is then a vocative with the particle of address omitted. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: The apparent sense from the law of Moses is that he was sent to call Pharaoh to faith and to ask that he send the Children of Israel. When Pharaoh refused to believe, the contention over sending the Children of Israel became firm. He said: What indicates this is His saying afterwards: ﴿And if you do not believe in me, then withdraw from me﴾.

His saying ﴿Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger﴾ is the reason for the command to hand over the Children of Israel to him, that is: because I am sent to you with this, and I am trustworthy, that is, entrusted concerning my being a messenger to you.

The placing of "to you" before "messenger" is for emphasis on the sending being connected to them first, by their handing over the Children of Israel to him, because that is a means to the purpose of his being sent, namely to liberate the nation of Israel and to legislate for it. The phrase "to you" is not an address to the Children of Israel, for Moses had already conveyed his message to the Children of Israel along with conveying it to Pharaoh. He said: ﴿But none believed in Moses except some of his people, out of fear of Pharaoh and their chiefs, lest he trouble them﴾ [Q. 10:83]. It is also so that Pharaoh's refusal to release the Children of Israel would be a justification for the Children of Israel's disengagement from obedience to Pharaoh and their flight from his land.

He conjoined to the request to hand over the Children of Israel a prohibition against arrogance in refusing to answer God's command, out of disdain at being lowered in the eyes of their people. So he said: ﴿And that you not exalt yourselves against God﴾, that is: do not exalt yourselves against His command or against His messenger. Since exalting oneself against the command of God and the command of His messenger is elevating oneself above the obligatory obedience to their Lord, they are treated as though they were exalting themselves against God.

﴿And that you not exalt yourselves﴾ is conjoined to ﴿that you deliver to me﴾. The explanatory "that" (an) is repeated to increase the emphasis of the explanation of the implication of "messenger". "Lā" is prohibitive, and the verb "ta'lū" is jussive by the prohibitive "lā".

The clause ﴿Indeed, I bring you a clear authority﴾ is a reason worthy of returning to the three preceding clauses, which are ﴿deliver to me the servants of God﴾, ﴿Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger﴾, and ﴿and that you not exalt yourselves against God﴾, because the miracle indicates the realisation of the contents of those clauses, as their effect and their cause.

Al-sulṭān is among the names of proof (ḥujja). He said: ﴿You have no authority for this﴾ [Q. 10:68]. Proof compels the one who is refuted to acknowledge the one who argues with him, so it is like one who holds power over himself.

The miracle is a great proof, and for this reason the authority is described as "clear" (mubīn), that is, evident in its indication, with no doubt about it. This miracle is the turning of his staff into a manifest serpent.

"Ātīkum" is either the present tense or the active participle of (atā). On both possibilities it requires bringing the proof in the present.

The clause ﴿And indeed I have sought refuge in my Lord﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿deliver to me the servants of God﴾, for the content of this clause is among what his speech included at the time of conveying his message, so it was included in the general sense of ﴿and there came to them a noble messenger﴾, which is explained by what follows the explanatory "that".

Its meaning is a warning to them not to stone him, because the meaning of ﴿I have sought refuge in my Lord﴾ is: I have made my Lord a refuge (ʿawdh), that is, a place of safety. The expression is a metaphor by comparing the reminder of the fear of God, which keeps them from aggression against him, with taking refuge in a fortress or stronghold, through the common feature of safety from aggression. Expressions like this have become proverbial. Among them is His saying in Surat Maryam: ﴿She said, "Indeed, I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you, if you are God-fearing"﴾ [Q. 19:18]. One of the rajaz poets of the Arabs said:

"She said, while in her there was shying and terror: 'A refuge in my Lord from you, and a sanctuary.'"

The expression of God with the description "my Lord and your Lord" is because He was brought into their restraint from stoning him, when they recall that he sought protection in God, whose lordship they share, and that they do not step outside His power.

to them. So the implied sense is: "they did not respond to him in what he commanded them," or "they persisted in harming him and in not leaving him alone, so he called upon his Lord." This is like the sequence in His exalted words ﴿So We revealed to Musa: "Strike the sea with your staff," and it parted﴾ [ash-Shu'ara': 63], and His words ﴿Indeed, these are a people who are criminals.﴾ All ten readers agree on reciting it with a fatha on the hamza and a shadda on the nun, so that what follows it is in the position of a verbal noun (masdar). Therefore the preposition bi (bi, "with") through which the verb (da'a, "called") is transitive is to be understood as implied, meaning: he called upon his Lord with what this construction comprises, used in the sense of allusion, that they had merited the imposition of the punishment which the one calling upon God seeks. Let me translate the passage now.

It is an *'atf* (conjunction) on the clause ﴿So travel by night with My servants﴾ [al-Dukhan: 23]. The two clauses may have been spoken consecutively, in that God informed Moses, when He commanded him to travel by night, that he would strike the sea with his staff, and it would split open, its dry bed exposed, so that the Children of Israel could pass through it, as is reported in other verses, such as the verse in Surat al-Shu'ara'. When He commanded him to do this, He reassured him that he need not fear that it would remain split, so that he would expect Pharaoh to catch up with him. Rather, he would cross the sea and leave it, for He would overpower Pharaoh and his army, and they would drown. In the speech there is thus an ellipsis (*ijaz*), whose implied meaning is: "When you have set out with My servants, We will open the sea for you, and you will pass through it. When you have passed through it, do not fear that Pharaoh and his army will overtake you, and leave it, for they are going to drown in it."

It is also possible that the second clause was spoken at the time when Moses and those with him entered the paths of the sea. In that case an implied speech is understood: "And We said to him: ﴿leave the sea parted﴾," meaning: Pharaoh and his army will enter it and will not come out of it, for there is another wisdom in its remaining divided, namely the entry of Pharaoh and his army into its paths, out of their desire to overtake Moses and his people. Then, when they reached its middle, it closed over them. Thus the benefit of the Children of Israel's deliverance and the benefit of the destruction of their enemy are both achieved. In this case the *waw* is a conjunction linking an implied speech to the implied speech before it.

On both interpretations, *al-tark* (leaving) is used figuratively to mean not caring about something, as one says: "Let him do such-and-such," and "Leave him (*dhurhu*)." This is like the words of God, ﴿Leave them in their discourse, playing﴾ [al-An'am: 91]. Kabsha bint Ma'd Yakrib said:

"Leave Amr aside, for Amr is at peace;
is the belly of Amr anything but a morsel's span?"

The sea is the Sea of Qulzum, today called the Red Sea.

*Al-Rahw* is a wide gap. Its origin is the verbal noun of *raha*, meaning he opened the space between his legs, and so the gap was called *rahwan* by using the verbal noun as a name. *Rahwan* is in the accusative as a *hal* (circumstantial qualifier) of "the sea," by way of an eloquent simile (*tashbih baligh*), meaning "like a gap."

The clause ﴿Indeed they are an army that will be drowned﴾ is an explanatory resumptive clause (*istinaf bayani*), answering a question arising from the command to leave the sea open. The pronoun "they" in ﴿indeed they﴾ refers back to the demonstrative in His words ﴿Indeed these are a people who are criminals﴾ [al-Dukhan: 22]. *Jund* means a people, a nation, and a king's army.

The insertion of the word *jund* (army), rather than limiting the description to "will be drowned," serves to convey that their drowning had become so inherent to them that it was as if it were one of the constituents of their identity, as we have already explained at His words ﴿there are signs for a people who reason﴾ in Surat al-Baqara.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 44, verses 25–27:

﴿How many gardens and springs they left behind﴾ ﴿and cornfields and noble dwellings﴾ ﴿and comfort in which they took delight﴾ ﴿Thus [it was]﴾ [al-Dukhan: 28]

This is a fresh, independent resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i), brought to draw a lesson from the ends of the wrongdoers who were deluded by the blessing and power they enjoyed, a delusion that made them forget being mindful of God in what pleases Him. The position of this resumption is that of a conclusion drawn from evidence, or an elaboration of the general comparison in His saying ﴿And We had already tried before them the people of Pharaoh﴾ [al-Dukhan: 17].

The pronoun in "tarakū" (they left) refers back to what the pronoun in ﴿Indeed, they are a drowned army﴾ [al-Dukhan: 24] refers to.

The literal meaning of "tark" (leaving) is placing something in a place and departing from it, leaving it there by choice. It is used figuratively for departing from a place and from a thing that is in a place of domination, without choice. This is a well-known figurative usage: "the deceased left (taraka) wealth," and from it the property a dead person leaves behind is called "tarikah" (inheritance). It is of this kind here.

The verb "tarakū" indicates that they were drowned and destroyed. This follows from the fact that what God commanded Moses concerning the journey by night with the Children of Israel, what accompanied it of Pharaoh following them, the splitting of the sea, the bringing near of the Children of Israel, Pharaoh's plunging into the sea with his armies, and the sea closing over them had all come to pass. So the speech is concise, omitting many sentences, which "how many they left" points to.

"Kam" (how many) is a noun denoting an indefinite large number, whose kind is specified by a following noun in the accusative of specification (tamyiz) governed by "min" (of), which is either stated or omitted.

"Kam" takes the grammatical treatment of nouns, depending on the governing words. Since it has the front position in the sentence, because originally it is interrogative, it cannot be the predicate of a subject, nor the predicate of "kana" or "inna." When it is governed by verbs, it must be placed before its governor.

"Kam" here is in the accusative as the direct object of "tarakū," meaning: they left many gardens. "Min" is the particle specifying the indefinite number in "kam."

"Maqam," with a fathah on the mim, is the place of standing, and "standing" here is used figuratively to mean being settled in a place.

"Karim" of every kind means its finest and best, and what is meant by it is the dwellings, homes, markets and the like that they had in the city of (Manfisin).

"Ni'mah," with a fathah on the nun, is a noun for enjoyment of blessings, patterned on the form of the single instance. It does not mean a single instance but the verbal noun in general, on the basis that the totality of the states of blessing has become like one thing; this is more eloquent and comprehensive in depicting the meaning of the verbal noun, and this is what suits the verb "tarakū," because what is left behind is the individual matters through which one is blessed, not the abstract verbal meaning.

"Fakihin" means those characterized by fukahah (with a dammah on the fa'), which is play and jest; that is, they were immersed in blessing, playing in that blessing.

Qur'an readers differ on this word. The majority read "fakihin" in the form of the active participle. Hafs and Abu Ja'far read "fakihin" without an alif, as an adjective of the attributive (sifah mushabbahah) type.

The indication is to an implied element that the speech points to, together with the meaning of the kaf. This construction was already discussed under His saying ﴿Thus [it was]. And We encompassed what was with him in knowledge﴾ [al-Kahf: 91] in Surat al-Kahf.

﴿And We caused a different people to inherit them﴾

This is an ʿaṭf (a grammatical coordination) upon "they left" (تركوا). The meaning is: they left it, and We made others inherit it, namely Pharaoh's successor who ruled after the death of Manfaṭā, called Ṣafṭā Manfaṭā, who was one of Pharaoh's commanders. He married Manfaṭā's daughter, named Ṭūsīr, who succeeded her father (Manfaṭā) on the throne of Egypt. Because he was not of Pharaoh's lineage, he and his army were described as "a different people." The intended meaning of ﴿a different people﴾ is not a people from the Children of Israel. Do you not see that the explicit noun was repeated in the following words, ﴿And We had certainly delivered the Children of Israel﴾ [al-Dukhan: 30], and He did not say "And We had certainly delivered them."

In the verse of al-Shuʿarāʾ occurs ﴿So We expelled them from gardens and springs﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 57], ﴿and treasures and a noble station﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 58], ﴿Thus, and We caused the Children of Israel to inherit them﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 59]. The meaning there is that various kinds of what We expelled the people of Pharaoh from, We caused the Children of Israel to inherit, and it was not intended that these kinds of things were specifically in the land of Pharaoh. The relevance of that there is that the two peoples were expelled from what they had been in. One of the two groups lost what it possessed, without return, because they were destroyed, and the other group was given similar things in the land of Palestine. So in His saying ﴿and We caused them to inherit﴾ there is an eloquent tashbīh (a forceful figure of comparison). Consult the verse of Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 44, verse 29:

﴿So the heaven and the earth did not weep for them, nor were they reprieved.﴾ This is a consequence (tafri') of His saying ﴿How many gardens did they leave behind?﴾ [al-Dukhan: 25] up to His saying ﴿and other people.﴾ [al-Dukhan: 28]. All of that implies that they perished and were wiped out, meaning: their destruction was no different from the destruction of others, and it was not a momentous event as they and their people supposed. It was among the usages of the Arabs that when a great person died they would magnify the matter of his death with expressions such as: "the sky wept for him," "the wind wept for him," and "the mountains shook." Al-Nabigha said, anticipating the death of al-Nu'man ibn al-Mundhir from his illness:

﴿If Abu Qabus perishes, the spring of the people and the sacred land will perish.﴾

And he said in lamenting al-Nu'man ibn al-Harith al-Ghassani:

Harith al-Jawlan wept over the loss of his lord, *** and Hawran, bereft of him, is desolate and diminished.

Page 304

The speech is directed in the manner of belittling them. It is close to His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and though their plot were such that the mountains would thereby be moved﴾ [Ibrahim: 46]. This is a well-trodden path, and such usage is frequent in the poetry of the later poets. Abu Bakr ibn al-Labbana al-Andalusi said in lamenting al-Mu'tamid ibn 'Abbad, king of Seville:

The sky weeps with a passing, morning cloud *** over the noble ones, the sons of 'Abbad.

The meaning is: their destruction was no different from the destruction of others, and they were not given respite by delaying their destruction; rather, their annihilation was hastened for them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 44, verses 30–31:

﴿And We certainly delivered the Children of Israel from the humiliating punishment﴾ ﴿from Pharaoh. Indeed, he was haughty among the transgressors﴾.

It is conjoined (ma'tuf) to the omitted discourse indicated by His saying ﴿Indeed, they are an army that will be drowned﴾ [al-Dukhan: 24]. Its implied meaning is: "So We drowned them, and We delivered the Children of Israel," as He said in Surat al-Shu'ara': ﴿And We brought near there the others﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 64], ﴿And We delivered Moses and those with him, all of them﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 65], ﴿Then We drowned the others﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 66].

The meaning is: "And We delivered the Children of Israel from the punishment of Pharaoh and his cruelty," that is, the sign of the sea was destruction for one people and deliverance for others.

The purpose of mentioning this is to point out that God, exalted is He, delivers those who believe in Muhammad (ﷺ) from the punishment of the polytheists in Mecca, just as He delivered those who followed Moses from the punishment of Pharaoh.

The tyranny of Pharaoh and his excess in evil were made an example of the tyranny of Abu Jahl and his chieftains. For the sake of this indication, the report is emphasized with the lam (of emphasis). It may also serve to affirm the deliverance of the believers from the punishment decreed for the disbelievers, in response to their supplication: ﴿Our Lord, remove from us the punishment; indeed, we are believers﴾ [al-Dukhan: 12].

"The humiliating punishment" is what Pharaoh and his people inflicted upon them of enslavement and oppression in forced labour. He used to require them to make bricks every day for the building of his two cities, Faythum and Ra'amses. The bricks were made of mud and straw, so he required them to bring in the straw needed for making bricks, and they would gather its scattered remnants, and they humiliated them and gave them no rest. That punishment is "humiliating" because it is a punishment containing degradation.

Page 305

As for His saying ﴿from Pharaoh﴾, the more apparent view is that it is a substitute (badal) that corresponds exactly to "the humiliating punishment," so the (min) here serves as an intensifier of the first (min) which governs "delivered" (najjayna). This is because the particle that enters upon the substituted-from noun may also enter upon the substitute for emphasis. This is good in view of subtleties that the context requires, and its goodness here is that (min) was made explicit because the fact that Pharaoh's name is a substitute for the punishment is hidden, as an alert to the intention of magnifying the matter of Pharaoh by making his very name the humiliating punishment, that is, as being issued from Pharaoh.

The clause ﴿Indeed, he was haughty﴾ is a resumed explanatory clause (isti'naf bayani) to clarify the magnification conveyed by making Pharaoh's name a substitute for the humiliating punishment. "Haughty" (ali): the arrogant, the great in power, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, Pharaoh exalted himself in the land﴾ [al-Qasas: 4].

﴿Among the transgressors﴾ is a second predicate about Pharaoh. "Israf" means excess and abundance. What is intended here is abundance in self-exaltation, and it is understood as abundance in wrongdoing by the indication of the context of censure.

﴿Among the transgressors﴾ is more emphatic in describing him with transgression than saying "transgressing" (musrifan), as was mentioned earlier in His saying ﴿He said: I seek refuge in God from being among the ignorant﴾ [al-Baqarah: 67] in Surat al-Baqarah.

*"Indeed I, with what I know of envy, am a man who is hated and despised with hostility and malice."*

By "the worlds" (العالَمِينَ) is meant the nations contemporary with them. Then they changed after that, so humiliation was struck upon them. God chose the Companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) over the nations, saying, ﴿You are the best nation raised up for mankind﴾ [Ali ʿImran: 110], that is, God raised them up for mankind.

As for the Muslims after them, they were chosen in a relative sense, according to the measure of their uprightness and the uprightness of other nations, given that monotheism (*al-tawḥīd*) is not equalled by anything.
