Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 44, verses 33–34:

"﴿And We gave them of the signs that which contained a manifest trial.﴾"

The giving of signs is among the effects of choice (al-ikhtiyar), because it is part of Allah's care for the community, since it increases them in certainty (yaqin) through their faith.

What is meant by "the signs" (al-ayat) are the miracles (al-mu'jizat) that appeared at the hand of Musa (peace be upon him), with which Allah strengthened the Children of Israel in their battles, by granting victory to the small group among them over the large armies of their enemy.

This is an allusion (ta'ridh) and a warning to the polytheists that the Muslims would overcome their large host despite their small number, as at Badr and elsewhere.

Al-bala' (trial, affliction) is testing, and it occurs through good and through evil. The first is a test of how one responds to a blessing, with gratitude or otherwise, and the second is a test of the measure of patience. The Exalted said: ﴿And We test you with evil and with good as a trial﴾ [al-Anbiya': 35], meaning that it contains a test for them in the eyes of the people, so that some may know that they met the blessing of the giving of signs with gratitude, and so that they might warn their people against meeting the blessing with ingratitude.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 44, verses 35–36:

﴿Indeed, these people are saying﴾ [al-Dukhan: 34] ﴿"There is nothing but our first death, and we shall not be resurrected. So bring back our fathers, if you are truthful."﴾

This is a parenthetical statement (i'tiraD) placed between the clause "the Day We seize with the greatest seizure, indeed We will take retribution" and the clause ﴿Are they better, or the people of Tubba'?﴾ [al-Dukhan: 37]. When He threatened them with the punishment of the smoke, then with the greatest seizure, and set forth for them the example of the people of Pharaoh, He followed this with an indication that their denial of resurrection is what diverted them from expecting the recompense of evil for their aversion.

The opening of the speech with the particle (inna), which is not for emphasis, because this statement addressed to the polytheists is not open to doubt such that it would need emphasis, so it is determined that the particle (inna) serves merely to draw attention to the information. When it occurs in such a position, it conveys causation and dispenses with the particle (fa). The meaning is: "Indeed, We will take retribution against them with the greatest seizure, because they are not restrained by the threat of the Hereafter, due to their denial of the Hereafter. They only look at what they have in the life of this world of blessing and power, and therefore God has decreed for them the recompense for the evil of their disbelief as a recompense in the life of this world."

The pronoun in (hiya) is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamir al-sha'n), which is also called the pronoun of the story (ḍamir al-qiṣṣa), because it is used in the feminine form in accordance with the interpretation of "the story." That is, in this matter there is no story except the well-known death, so it is a single death after which there is no resurrection for us.

This is one of their statements in denying resurrection, for they have several statements on this. At times they deny that there is any life after death, as God related of them in other verses, such as His saying ﴿And they say: There is nothing but our life of this world﴾ [al-An'am: 29]. At other times they deny that anything befalls them after the well-known death other than it, meaning by this something opposite to death, which is life after death.

This is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*, a new sentence that follows on from what precedes it), following His words, ﴿And We had already tested before them the people of Pharaoh﴾ (al-Dukhan 44:17). The pronoun in "*hum*" (them) refers back to the demonstrative in His words, ﴿Indeed, these say﴾ (al-Dukhan 44:34), ﴿There is only our first death﴾ (al-Dukhan 44:35). So after the example of the destruction of the people of Pharaoh had been set forth for them, He added another example, one closer to their consideration of it: the destruction of a people nearer to their lands than the people of Pharaoh. These were the people of Tubba'. The Arabs had heard of the greatness of the king Tubba' and his people, the people of Yemen, and many of the Arabs had seen the remains of their strength and greatness during the stages of their journeys, and they had talked about what befell them of destruction by the flood of al-Arim (*Sayl al-Arim*).

The speech opens with an interrogation of affirmation (*istifham taqriri*, a question whose answer is already known and is meant to affirm), in order to draw attention to its content, because everyone knows that Tubba' and those kings before him were better than these polytheists.

The meaning is: they are not better than the people of Tubba' and those nations before them whom God uprooted because of their criminality. When they are equal to them in criminality, then they have no superiority that would ward off from them the same annihilation with which God destroyed the nations before them.

The interrogation in ﴿Are they better, or the people of Tubba'?﴾ is an affirmation, since they can do nothing but acknowledge that the people of Tubba' and those before them were better than them, because they used to cite them as examples of strength. The meaning of "better" here is superiority in strength and power, as He said, after mentioning the people of Pharaoh, ﴿Are your unbelievers better than those?﴾ (al-Qamar 54:43) in Surah al-Qamar.

The people of Tubba' are the Himyar, who were the inhabitants of Yemen and Hadramawt, from Himyar and Saba'. God mentioned them in Surah Qaf.

*Tubba'*, with a *damma* on the *ta'* and a shadda on the *ba'*, is a title for one who rules all the lands of Yemen: Himyar, Saba' and Hadramawt. Thus the title Tubba' is applied to a king only if he rules these three regions. It is said that they called him Tubba' after the shadow, because it follows the sun just as the shadow follows the sun, and the meaning of that is that he travelled with his campaigns to every place the sun rises upon, as God said of Dhu al-Qarnayn, ﴿So he followed a way until, when he reached the setting place of the sun﴾ (al-Kahf 18:85), to His words, ﴿We had not made for them any shelter from it﴾ (al-Kahf 18:90). It is also said that he was named so because the kings of the *makhalif* of Yemen followed him, and all the *aqyal* and *adhwa'* (chieftains) of the kings of the *makhalif* of Yemen and its *adhwa'* submitted to him; therefore he was titled Tubba' because kings followed him.

Tubba' here refers to the one named As'ad and known by the kunya Abu Karib. His dominion became great, he campaigned against the lands of the Arabs, entered Makkah and Yathrib, and reached Iraq. It is said that he was the one who built the city of al-Hira in Iraq. The reign of Tubba' was about a thousand years before the Muhammadan mission, and it has been said that it was around seven hundred years before the mission of the Prophet (ﷺ).

The fact that the destruction is attributed to the people of Tubba' and not to him implies that Tubba' escaped this destruction, and that the destruction was imposed upon his people. 'A'isha said: "Do you not see that God censured his people but did not censure him?"

What is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) in the *Musnad* of Ahmad and others is that he said: "Do not revile Tubba', for he had embraced Islam." In another narration: "He was a believer." Some scholars explained this as meaning that he was upon the religion of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), and that he was guided to that through the company of two rabbis of the Jewish rabbis whom he met in Yathrib when he campaigned against it. That implies his deliverance from the destruction. Perhaps God destroyed his people after his death or during his absence.

The clause ﴿We destroyed them﴾ is a resumptive sentence of explanation (*isti'naf bayani*), in response to what the interrogation of affirmation raised, namely the question about its ambiguity: what was intended by it.

The clause ﴿Indeed, they were criminals﴾ is a reason (*ta'lil*) for the content of the clause ﴿We destroyed them﴾. That is: We destroyed them utterly, root and branch, because of their criminality, that is, their polytheism.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 44, verse 38–39:

﴿And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play.﴾ ﴿We did not create them except with truth, but most of them do not know.﴾

It is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the sentence ﴿Indeed, these say﴾ [al-Dukhan: 34] ﴿There is only our first death﴾ [al-Dukhan: 35], as a rebuttal to them, as you have just come to know. The meaning is: if there were no resurrection and recompense, the creation of the heavens and the earth and what is between them would be in vain (ʿabath). But We created all of that with truth (haqq), that is, with wisdom (hikmah), as the perfection of the order of existing things indicates. Therefore, the creation of that necessarily requires that every doer be recompensed for his deed and that this not be lost. Since it is observed that many people spend their lives without seeing any recompense for their actions, it is established that God has delayed their recompense to another life; otherwise their creation, in some of its states, would be of the kind of play (laʿib).

The mention of play is a rebuke to those who denied resurrection and recompense, since they hold a belief that leads to making the actions of the Wise into play. The basis of this implication has already been explained at the exegesis of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Did you think that We created you in vain and that you would not be returned to Us?﴾ [al-Muminun: 115] in Surat al-Muminun, and at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vain. That is the assumption of those who disbelieved﴾ [Sad: 27] in Surat Sad.

"Laʿibin" (playing) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "khalaqna" (We created), and the negation is directed at this circumstance. It therefore requires the negation of any part of that creation being in a state of play, and among that is the state of neglecting recompense.

The sentence ﴿We did not create them except with truth﴾ is a substitutive clause of inclusion (badal ishtimal) from the sentence ﴿We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play﴾.

The preposition "bi" in "bil-haqq" denotes accompaniment (mulabasah), meaning We created that accompanied by and joined with truth; or the "bi" denotes causation (sababiyyah), meaning on account of truth, that is, for the sake of bringing about the truth from their creation.

Al-haqq is that which must occur of an action or a statement, that is, that which is necessary and determined by way of causation, consequence, or recompense. Among the truth for which the heavens and the earth and what is between them were created is the requital of every doer with what suits his deed and the compensating of him. This was already discussed at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Do they not reflect within themselves? God did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except with truth﴾ [al-Rum: 8] in Surat al-Rum.

The istidrak (contrastive turn) in His saying ﴿but most of them do not know﴾ arises from what the negation of creation being play, and the affirmation that it is for truth alone, has conveyed: that the matter of this is not hidden. But the ignorance of the polytheists is what led them to say: "We shall not be raised" (ma nahnu bi-mansharin).

The sentence of istidrak is a concluding summation (tadhyil), and close in meaning to this verse is His saying ﴿We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except with truth, and the Hour is certainly coming﴾ [al-Hijr: 85] at the end of Surat al-Hijr.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 44, verses 40–42:

﴿Indeed, the Day of Decision is their appointed time, all of them.﴾ ﴿The Day when no kinsman will avail another kinsman at all, nor will they be helped.﴾ ﴿Except for whom Allah has shown mercy. Indeed, He is the Mighty, the Merciful.﴾ This sentence descends from the one before it in the position of the conclusion (*natijah*) of an argument (*istidlal*), and for this reason it is not joined by a conjunction. The meaning is: "So the Day of Decision is their appointed time," as an announcement to them that the Day of Judgment is the final term of recompense. Thus it is a threat to them and a confirmation of the report, in response to their denial.

"The Day of Decision" is the Day of Judgment, because on it truth is separated from falsehood. It is also one of the names of the Day of Resurrection. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿To what Day has it been postponed?﴾ [Al-Mursalat: 12] ﴿For the Day of Decision.﴾ [Al-Mursalat: 13]

"Al-miqat" (appointed time): the noun of time of appointment, i.e., of postponement. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, the Day of Decision was an appointed time.﴾ [An-Naba': 17]. It was discussed at His saying ﴿They ask you about the new moons. Say: they are signs for the people and for Hajj.﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 189] in Surat al-Baqarah. The complement of "al-miqat" is omitted because it is evident from the context, meaning: the appointed time of their recompense.

The "appointed time" is attributed to the pronoun of those being addressed about, because they are the intended target of this threat. Otherwise, the Day of Decision is the appointed time of all creation, believers and disbelievers alike.

The emphasis by "ajma'in" (all of them) is to make explicit the comprehensiveness and inclusiveness, meaning: an appointed time for their recompense, all of them, none of them escaping from it, as a strengthening of the threat and a removal of hope regarding any exception.

﴿The Day when no kinsman will avail another kinsman﴾: this is a substitute (*badal*) for "the Day of Decision," or an explicative apposition (*'atf bayan*). The vowel-fatha on "yawma la yughni" is the fatha of inflection (*fathat i'rab*), because "yawm" is annexed to a clause containing an inflected verb.

"Al-mawla" means the close relative and the ally. It was discussed at Allah's saying ﴿And indeed I fear my kinsmen (*al-mawali*) after me.﴾ [Maryam: 5] in Surat Maryam. The indefiniteness of "mawla" in the context of negation is to convey generality, meaning: no kinsman whatsoever will avail any of his kinsmen whatsoever.

"Shay'an" (anything) is an absolute object (*maf'ul mutlaq*), because what is meant is "a degree of availing." The indefiniteness of "shay'an" is for diminution, which is the prevalent use of indefinite "shay'" as in Allah's saying ﴿and something of a few lote-trees﴾ [Saba': 16]. Its occurrence in the context of negation also conveys generality, meaning: any availing at all, however little, let alone great availing. The meaning is: the Day when their kinsmen will not avail them; but He turned from that to generalization because it is broader in benefit, as it functions as a concluding generalization (*tadhyil*).

"Al-Igha'" (availing) means benefit and profit, whether much or little. The two pronouns in "wa la hum yunsaruna" refer to what the pronoun in "ahum" (them) refers back to, which is the demonstrative from Allah's saying ﴿Indeed, these are surely saying﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 34]. The meaning is: their supporters, who are presumed to be of that kind, will not avail them, and other companions assigned to them, who are not among their kinsmen, will not help them, even if moved by zeal, jealousy, or compassion so that they come to their aid.

"Al-Nasr" (help) is aid against an enemy and against the dominant party, and it is the strongest form of availing.

Thus "wa la hum yunsaruna" is conjoined to "la yughni mawlan 'an mawlan shay'an" as an increase in the negation of availing.

The sum of the meaning, then, is that no kinsman avails his kinsman with anything of availing according to his capacity, and no helper with strong capacity, who is stronger than them, will repel from them the overpowering of the mighty over them. Allah is the Overpowering, and none overpowers Him.

The verb "yunsaruna" is constructed in the passive voice in order to encompass the negation of every helper, together with brevity of expression.

[Page 313]

The exception with Allah's saying ﴿except for whom Allah has shown mercy﴾ comes directly after the two clauses ﴿no kinsman will avail another kinsman at all, nor will they be helped﴾, so it is fitting that it refer back to what is suitable for exception from those two clauses. In the two clauses there are three terms suitable to be excepted from: the first "mawla," the nominative subject of "yughni"; the second "mawla," the genitive after the preposition "'an"; and the pronoun in "wa la hum yunsaruna." Therefore the exception with respect to these three is a connected exception (*istithna' muttasil*), meaning: except for the kinsman whom Allah has shown mercy, that is, He permits intercession for him, and permits the intercessor to intercede, as Allah said ﴿and intercession will not benefit with Him except for one whom He has permitted﴾ [Saba': 23], and He said ﴿and they do not intercede except for one with whom He is pleased﴾ [Al-Anbiya': 28]. In the hadith of intercession it is said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Ask, and you will be given; intercede, and your intercession will be accepted." Intercession is availing with respect to the one interceded for. The intercessors on that Day are allies of the believers, since among the intercessors are the angels, and Allah has related their saying to the believers: ﴿We are your allies in the life of this world and in the Hereafter.﴾ [Fussilat: 31]

It has also been said that it is a disjunctive exception (*istithna' munqati'*), because the one whom Allah has shown mercy is not included in anything before him that refers to the people of the gathering. The meaning is: "But whoever Allah has shown mercy does not need anyone to avail him or help him." This is the view of al-Kisa'i and al-Farra'.

The causes of Allah's mercy are many, and they return to His pleasure with His servant, and that is a secret which Allah knows.

The sentence ﴿Indeed, He is the Mighty, the Merciful﴾ is an explanatory resumption (*isti'naf bayani*), which is a general answer to a questioner asking about the specification of whom Allah has shown mercy. The meaning is: Allah is Mighty, no one compels Him to deviate from His will; He shows mercy to whomever He wills by His sheer will; and He is the Merciful, that is, of vast mercy to whomever He wills of His servants, in accordance with what has already been decreed by His knowledge, His wisdom, and His promise. In the hadith: "Show mercy to those on earth, and He who is in heaven will show mercy to you."

"﴿Indeed, the tree of Zaqqum, the food of the sinner, is like murky oil; it boils in the bellies like the boiling of scalding water. Seize him and drag him into the midst of the Blazing Fire. Then pour over his head some of the torment of scalding water. Taste it; indeed, you were the mighty, the noble. Indeed, this is what you used to doubt.﴾

When God mentioned a group of those who receive mercy in general terms, He here set against them a group who are punished, namely the polytheists, and described some kinds of their punishment: their food, their humiliation, and their burning. The expected form would have been to begin by informing about them that they eat from the tree of Zaqqum, as He said in Surat al-Waqi'ah: ﴿Then indeed you, O astray deniers, will be eaters from a tree of Zaqqum﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 56:51], and so on. Instead, He turned away from that and informed about the tree of Zaqqum that it is the food of the sinner, out of concern to make known the state of this tree. The tree of Zaqqum has been made something known to the listeners, so it was referred to by the definite form of the construct phrase (ta'rif al-idafah), because its mention had already preceded in Surat al-Waqi'ah, which was revealed before Surat al-Dukhan. Al-Waqi'ah is counted as the forty-sixth in the order of the revelation of the surahs, and Surat al-Dukhan is the sixty-third.

The meaning of the tree being food is that its fruit is food, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Its shoot is as if it were the heads of devils﴾ [al-Saffat 37:65], ﴿and indeed they will eat from it﴾ [al-Saffat 37:66].

The common practice in the orthography of word endings is that the state of pausing (hal al-waqf) be observed in it, so this is among the cases that came contrary to the original rule.

Al-athim (الأثيم) means one who commits many sins, as the pattern of the form fa'il indicates. This is an instance of using an explicit noun in place of a pronoun (al-idhar fi maqam al-idmar), with the purpose of hinting that their association of partners with God, together with its cause, is what makes their treatment like this.

[Page 315]

The discussion of the tree of Zaqqum has already preceded in Surat al-Saffat, at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Is that better as a welcome, or the tree of Zaqqum?﴾ [al-Saffat 37:62].

Al-muhl (المهل), with a dammah on the mim, is the sediment of oil (duradi al-zayt). The comparison with it is in the blackness of its colour, and it was also said that it is in its melting.

Al-hamim (الحميم) is water of extreme heat that has finished boiling. It was discussed earlier at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿For them is a drink of scalding water﴾ [al-An'am 6:70], in Surat al-An'am. The aspect of resemblance is the form of its boiling.

The majority read "تَغْلِي" (taghli) with the upper ta' (ta' fawqiyyah), with the pronoun referring to the tree of Zaqqum. The attribution of boiling to the tree is metaphorical (majaz), since what actually boils is its fruit. Ibn Kathir and Hafs read it with the lower ya' (ya' tahtiyyah), with the pronoun referring back to the food (al-ta'am), not to al-muhl.

Al-ghalayan (الغليان) is the intense effect of heat of fire upon a thing. It is said: "ghalā al-mā'u" (the water boiled) and "ghalat al-qidr" (the pot boiled). Al-Nabighah said:

"Al-Nu'man travels with them, his cooking pots boiling."

The clause "khudhuhu" (خذوه) and what follows is a speech (maqul) of an omitted saying indicated by the context. That is, it is said to the angels of punishment: "Seize him." The singular pronoun refers to the sinner in terms of the individuals of his kind.

Al-'atl (العتل) is driving forcefully, which is to be seized by the collar of someone and led to prison or punishment. Its past tense comes with a dammah or a kasrah on the ayn.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read it with a dammah. The rest read it with a kasrah on the ta'.

Sawa' al-shay' (سواء الشيء) is its middle, and it is the most intensely hot place.

His saying, "ila sawa' al-jahim" (إلى سواء الجحيم), is governed by each of the two verbs, "khudhuhu fa'tilu hu" (خذوه فاعتلوه), because both imply: drive him with violent driving.

The "thumma" (ثم) indicates a graded sequence (al-tarakhi al-rutbi), because pouring scalding water over his head is more severe for him than seizing him and dragging him.

Al-sabb (الصب) is pouring out a thing contained from its container. The verb "pour" does not extend to torment, because torment is an abstract matter that cannot be poured. So "pouring" is used figuratively for intensification and haste, and it is therefore an image (tamthiliyyah),

[Page 316]

required by the terror of the sinner when he hears it. Since what is related here is the speech that the sinner hears, it is phrased in the form of an image for the sake of awe. This differs from His saying: ﴿Scalding water will be poured over their heads﴾ [al-Hajj 22:19], which is information about them at a time when they are not hearing it, so this kind of metaphor was not used there, since there is no requirement for it.

The clause ﴿Taste it; indeed you were the mighty, the noble﴾ is the speech of another omitted saying, its estimate being: "Say to him," or "It is said to him."

Al-dhawq (الذوق) is used metaphorically for perception, and the imperative form is used to express humiliation.

His saying, ﴿indeed you were the mighty, the noble﴾, is a declarative statement used for mockery (al-tahakkum), through the relation of opposition (al-didiyyah). The intended meaning is the reverse of its literal denotation: you are the humbled and the abased. The emphasis serves the sense of mockery.

The majority read the hamzah of "innaka" with a kasrah. Al-Kisa'i read it with a fathah, on the estimate of the lam of causation and with the separate pronoun of the addressee in His saying "anta" (أنت) being an emphasis for the attached pronoun in "innaka". The attached accusative pronoun is not emphasized except by a separate nominative pronoun.

The clause ﴿Indeed, this is what you used to doubt﴾ is the remainder of the omitted saying, that is, and it is said to the sinners all together: "Indeed, this is what you used to doubt in the world." The declarative statement is used for reproach and rebuke. The demonstrative refers to the present state before them: this punishment and recompense is what you used to deny in the world.

The term imtira' has been applied to their firm conviction in denying the resurrection, because their certainty, being devoid of the indications of knowledge, was in the position of doubt. Al-hamim (الحميم) is water of extreme heat that has finished boiling. It was discussed earlier at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿For them is a drink of scalding water﴾ [al-An'am 6:70], in Surat al-An'am. The aspect of resemblance is the form of its boiling.

The majority read "تَغْلِي" (taghli) with the upper ta' (ta' fawqiyyah), with the pronoun referring to the tree of Zaqqum. The attribution of boiling to the tree is metaphorical (majaz), since what actually boils is its fruit. Ibn Kathir and Hafs read it with the lower ya' (ya' tahtiyyah), with the pronoun referring back to the food (al-ta'am), not to al-muhl.

Al-ghalayan (الغليان) is the intense effect of heat of fire upon a thing. It is said: "ghalā al-mā'u" (the water boiled) and "ghalat al-qidr" (the pot boiled). Al-Nabighah said:

"Al-Nu'man travels with them, his cooking pots boiling."

The clause "khudhuhu" (خذوه) and what follows is a speech (maqul) of an omitted saying indicated by the context. That is, it is said to the angels of punishment: "Seize him." The singular pronoun refers to the sinner in terms of the individuals of his kind.

Al-'atl (العتل) is driving forcefully, which is to be seized by the collar of someone and led to prison or punishment. Its past tense comes with a dammah or a kasrah on the ayn.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read it with a dammah. The rest read it with a kasrah on the ta'.

Sawa' al-shay' (سواء الشيء) is its middle, and it is the most intensely hot place.

His saying, "ila sawa' al-jahim" (إلى سواء الجحيم), is governed by each of the two verbs, "khudhuhu fa'tilu hu" (خذوه فاعتلوه), because both imply: drive him with violent driving.

The "thumma" (ثم) indicates a graded sequence (al-tarakhi al-rutbi), because pouring scalding water over his head is more severe for him than seizing him and dragging him.

Al-sabb (الصب) is pouring out a thing contained from its container. The verb "pour" does not extend to torment, because torment is an abstract matter that cannot be poured. So "pouring" is used figuratively for intensification and haste, and it is therefore an image (tamthiliyyah),

[Page 316]

required by the terror of the sinner when he hears it. Since what is related here is the speech that the sinner hears, it is phrased in the form of an image for the sake of awe. This differs from His saying: ﴿Scalding water will be poured over their heads﴾ [al-Hajj 22:19], which is information about them at a time when they are not hearing it, so this kind of metaphor was not used there, since there is no requirement for it.

The clause ﴿Taste it; indeed you were the mighty, the noble﴾ is the speech of another omitted saying, its estimate being: "Say to him," or "It is said to him."

Al-dhawq (الذوق) is used metaphorically for perception, and the imperative form is used to express humiliation.

His saying, ﴿indeed you were the mighty, the noble﴾, is a declarative statement used for mockery (al-tahakkum), through the relation of opposition (al-didiyyah). The intended meaning is the reverse of its literal denotation: you are the humbled and the abased. The emphasis serves the sense of mockery.

The majority read the hamzah of "innaka" with a kasrah. Al-Kisa'i read it with a fathah, on the estimate of the lam of causation and with the separate pronoun of the addressee in His saying "anta" (أنت) being an emphasis for the attached pronoun in "innaka". The clause ﴿Indeed, this is what you used to doubt﴾ is the remainder of the omitted saying, that is, and it is said to the sinners all together: "Indeed, this is what you used to doubt in the world." Al-imtira' (الامتراء) means doubt. The term imtira' has been applied to their firm conviction in denying the resurrection, because their certainty, being devoid of the indications of knowledge, was in the position of doubt. That is, the resurrection is of such a nature that one should not be certain in denying it, in the manner established in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿This is the Book, in which there is no doubt﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:2].

"﴿Indeed, the tree of Zaqqum, the food of the sinner, is like murky oil; it boils in the bellies like the boiling of scalding water. Seize him and drag him into the midst of the Blazing Fire. When God mentioned a group of those who receive mercy in general terms, He here set against them a group who are punished, namely the polytheists, and described some kinds of their punishment: their food, their humiliation, and their burning. The expected form would have been to begin by informing about them that they eat from the tree of Zaqqum, as He said in Surat al-Waqi'ah: ﴿Then indeed you, O astray deniers, will be eaters from a tree of Zaqqum﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 56:51], and so on. The tree of Zaqqum has been made something known to the listeners, so it was referred to by the definite form of the construct phrase (ta'rif al-idafah), because its mention had already preceded in Surat al-Waqi'ah, which was revealed before Surat al-Dukhan. Al-Waqi'ah is counted as the forty-sixth in the order of the revelation of the surahs, and Surat al-Dukhan is the sixty-third.

The meaning of the tree being food is that its fruit is food, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Its shoot is as if it were the heads of devils﴾ [al-Saffat 37:65], ﴿and indeed they will eat from it﴾ [al-Saffat 37:66].

The common practice in the orthography of word endings is that the state of pausing (hal al-waqf) be observed in it, so this is among the cases that came contrary to the original rule.

Al-athim (الأثيم) means one who commits many sins, as the pattern of the form fa'il indicates. This is an instance of using an explicit noun in place of a pronoun (al-idhar fi maqam al-idmar), with the purpose of hinting that their association of partners with God, together with its cause, is what makes their treatment like this.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 44, verses 51–53:

﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be in a secure place﴾ ﴿among gardens and springs﴾ ﴿They will wear fine silk and brocade, facing one another﴾

This is a new, independent sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i), by which the discourse moves from describing the punishment of the sinner to describing the bliss of the God-fearing, because of the contrast between them, in keeping with the Qur'an's custom of following a threat with a promise and vice versa.

Page 317
Al-muqam, with a dammah on the meem, is the place of residence; al-maqam, with a fathah on the meem, is the place of standing, and it includes the dwelling and what accompanies it.
Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Abu Ja'far read it with a dammah on the meem. The rest read it with a fathah on the meem.

The intended meaning of al-maqam is the place, so it is a metaphor (majaz) by the relation of particular and general ('alaqat al-khusus wal-'umum).

Al-amin means "the safe" (bi-ma'na al-aamin), and what is intended is that its dweller is safe. Describing the place as "amin" is therefore a metaphor in the intellectual sense (majaz 'aqli), as the Most High said: ﴿And this secure land﴾ [al-Tin: 3]. Security is the greatest of the conditions for a place's goodness, because the dweller first seeks security, which is freedom from what is disliked and feared. When he is safe in his dwelling, his mind is at ease and he feels the bliss he receives. The phrase is followed by an appositive (badal) with ﴿among gardens and springs﴾, which are among the means of enjoyment and pleasantness. The preposition "fi" is repeated with the appositive for emphasis.

Al-jannat is the plural of jannah, discussed at the beginning of al-Baqarah. Al-'uyun is the plural of 'ayn, discussed in His saying ﴿and there gushed forth from it twelve springs﴾ [al-Baqarah: 60] in Surat al-Baqarah. This is the bliss of their place. He described the bliss of their bodies by mentioning their clothing, which is the clothing of luxury and bliss, and in this there is an allusion (kinayah) to the abundance of the causes of bodily bliss, because one wears this clothing only if he has completed what precedes it of the comforts of the body, inwardly and outwardly.

Al-sundus is thin, precious brocade. Most scholars hold that it is arabicized from Persian, and it was said to be Arabic. Its origin is sindi, relating to al-Sind, by irregular derivation. Sundus is worn next to the body.

Al-istabraq is thick, strong brocade worn over garments. It is arabicized from the Persian "istabrah," which means thick in general, then it was restricted to thick brocade, and then it was arabicized.

Both were mentioned in His saying ﴿They will wear green garments of fine silk and brocade﴾ [al-Kahf: 31] in Surat al-Kahf, so refer back to it.

The "min" here is explicative (li-bayan al-jins), and the thing explained is omitted, indicated by "yalbasun." The estimated phrase is: garments of fine silk and brocade.

**﴿Thus﴾**

This is a parenthetical insertion (i‘tiraḍ). Its meaning has already been explained in His saying, ﴿Thus, and We encompassed what was with him in knowledge﴾ [al-Kahf: 91], in Surat al-Kahf. A similar instance occurred just before in this surah.

* * *

﴿And We will marry them to ḥūr ʿīn (maidens with wide, lustrous eyes)﴾ ﴿They will call for every kind of fruit therein, in security﴾ ﴿They will not taste death therein, except the first death﴾ [al-Dukhan: 54–56].

The meaning of "We will marry them" (zawwajnāhum) is "We will make them into pairs" (azwāj), the plural of zawj, the opposite of fard (single). That is, We will make each of the God-fearing a pair by means of women with lustrous eyes.

The word zawj here is a metaphorical expression (kināya) for a companion: We will pair each one with wide-eyed women. The verb zawwajnāhum here is not derived from the zawj commonly used for a man's wife or a woman's husband, because that verb takes a direct object, as in "he married him to his daughter" (zawwajahu ibnatahu) and "he married the daughter of so-and-so" (tazawwaja bint fulān). God says, ﴿We married her to you﴾ [al-Aḥzāb: 37]. That sense is not intended here, since it would serve no purpose: there are no marriage contracts in Paradise. What is meant is that they will be content in the company of beloved women, just as they were content in the company of companions and loved ones among men, completing the familiar comfort that people find with one another. In both kinds of companionship there is a spiritual delight that follows the soul from bodily pleasure. This is a noble meaning among the meanings of spiritual expansiveness. In this world, what spoils part of it is what mixes with it of circumstances that lead to forbidden corruption, such as committing what is unlawful in the Law and, like it, forcibly assaulting women,

Page 319

and of artificial terminologies. God has called it tranquility (sukūn), saying, ﴿And among His signs is that He created for you mates from yourselves, that you may find tranquility in them, and He placed between you affection and mercy﴾ [al-Rūm: 21].

Ḥūr is the plural of ḥawrāʾ, meaning "white" (bayḍāʾ), that is, women with very fair skin.

ʿĪn is the plural of ʿaynāʾ, meaning "wide-eyed" (wāsiʿat al-ʿayn). This was discussed in Surat al-Ṣāffāt. The ḥūr ʿīn include the women who were their wives in this world, and women whom God creates for the sake of Paradise. God says, ﴿Indeed, We created them with a special creation﴾ [al-Wāqiʿa: 35], and He says, ﴿They and their spouses are in shade﴾ [Yā-Sīn: 56].

The meaning of ﴿they will call for every kind of fruit therein﴾ is that they will order that fruit be brought to them, and they will be answered.

Calling (duʿāʾ) is a kind of command. That is, they will give permission for every kind of fruit, meaning for every kind of fruit to be brought.

"Every" (kull) here is used to express the very great abundance for each one of them. It may also mean comprehensiveness, that is, every category of fruit.

Fruit (fākiha) is what one enjoys, that is, what is savored for its taste, such as fruits and the like.

The clause "they will call" is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the God-fearing, and "in security" (āminīn) is a circumstantial clause relating to the pronoun in "they will call." What is meant here is a particular security, different from the one in His saying, ﴿in a secure place﴾ [al-Dukhan: 51]. This is security from harms and pains caused by those fruits, unlike the case of overeating in this world, as in His saying about the wine of Paradise, ﴿no headache comes from it, nor are they intoxicated by it﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 47]. Or it means secure from those things running out or ceasing.

The clause ﴿they will not taste death therein, except the first death﴾ [al-Dukhan: 56] is another circumstantial clause. This is good news of the everlasting continuance of the blessing, because death would cut off the pleasure that existed in life for the people of bliss, just as the announcement that the people of polytheism will not die is a warning of the perpetuity of punishment.

The exception in His saying ﴿except the first death﴾ [al-Dukhan: 56] is of the type that affirms a thing by means of something resembling its opposite, to intensify the negation of tasting death for the people of Paradise. It is as if it were said, "They will not taste death at all." The indication of this is the description of it as "the first." The meaning of "first" (al-ūlā) is "former," as was mentioned just before in His saying, ﴿It is only our first death﴾ [al-Dukhan: 35].

Surat al-Jathiyah

In al-Qurtubi, from Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah, is an exception: His words ﴿قُلْ لِلَّذِينَ آمَنُوا يَغْفِرُوا﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 14] "Say to those who believe that they should forgive," up to ﴿بِما كانُوا يَكْسِبُونَ﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 14] "for what they used to earn," were revealed in Medina. And from Ibn 'Abbas: it was revealed concerning 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) when a man of the polytheists insulted him in Mecca, so he wanted to seize him, and then it was revealed.

It is the sixty-fourth surah in the order of revelation of the surahs according to Jabir ibn Zayd. It was revealed after Surat al-Dukhan and before al-Ahqaf.

The number of its verses according to the counting of Medina, Mecca, Syria and Basra is thirty-six. According to the counting of Kufa it is thirty-seven, because of their disagreement over counting the letters "Ha-Mim" as a separate verse.

The denunciation of the polytheists for taking gods according to their own desires and for denying resurrection, and the warning to them of loss on the Day of Resurrection, and the description of its terrors and what has been prepared in it of punishment for the polytheists and of mercy for the believers.

It is also called "Surat al-Dahr," because His words ﴿وما يُهْلِكُنا إلّا الدَّهْرُ﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 24] "And nothing destroys us except time" occur in it, and the word "al-dahr" does not occur in the other sister surahs beginning with Ha-Mim.

It is a Meccan surah, according to Ibn 'Atiyyah who said: "without disagreement." In al-Qurtubi, from Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah, is an exception: His words ﴿قُلْ لِلَّذِينَ آمَنُوا يَغْفِرُوا﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 14] "Say to those who believe that they should forgive," up to ﴿بِما كانُوا يَكْسِبُونَ﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 14] "for what they used to earn," were revealed in Medina. And from Ibn 'Abbas: it was revealed concerning 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) when a man of the polytheists insulted him in Mecca, so he wanted to seize him, and then it was revealed.

It is the sixty-fourth surah in the order of revelation of the surahs according to Jabir ibn Zayd. It was revealed after Surat al-Dukhan and before al-Ahqaf.

The number of its verses according to the counting of Medina, Mecca, Syria and Basra is thirty-six. According to the counting of Kufa it is thirty-seven, because of their disagreement over counting the letters "Ha-Mim" as a separate verse.

* * *

Its purposes:

The opening with the challenge (tahaddi) concerning the miraculous nature of the Qur'an, and that it came with the truth, as a preparation for what will be mentioned, that it is true, as His words demand: ﴿تِلْكَ آياتُ اللَّهِ نَتْلُوها عَلَيْكَ بِالحَقِّ﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 6] "These are the verses of Allah, which We recite to you in truth."

The establishment of Allah's exclusive divinity through the evidences of what is in the heavens and the earth, of the traces of His creation and power in the substances of existing things and their accidents, and the inclusion with that of the blessings in them which deserve to be thanked by people, not denied.

The threat against those who lied against Allah, committed sins by persisting in disbelief, turned away from considering the verses of the Qur'an, and mocked them.

The denunciation of the polytheists for taking gods according to their own desires and for denying resurrection, and the warning to them of loss on the Day of Resurrection, and the description of its terrors and what has been prepared in it of punishment for the polytheists and of mercy for the believers.

The supplication of the Muslims to turn away from the harm the disbelievers inflict on them, and the promise that Allah will disgrace the polytheists.

The description of some conditions of the Day of Recompense. And the consideration of those who neglected to consider the signs of Allah, although they were made clear, and who opposed their Messenger (ﷺ) in what was good for them, by the state of the Children of Israel in their disagreement over their Book after knowledge had come to them and after they had followed it. So what is your opinion of one who opposes the signs of Allah from the very first moment? This is a warning to them lest they fall into what the Children of Israel fell into, of the domination of the nations over them, and that is a forceful warning.

This is also a confirmation to the Messenger (ﷺ) that the situation of his law with his people is like the situation of the law of Moses: it is not safe from an opponent, and that this does not discredit it nor the one who brought it, and that he should not pay attention to the obstinate ones nor to their multitude, since they have no weight with Allah.
